**Title:** Which Dollar Broke? Separating Token Failures from Platform-Ledger Failures in Web Dollar Markets

**Abstract (284 words):**

Crypto prices on the Web are quoted in two kinds of dollar: stablecoin tokens, and balances in an exchange's internal ledger that reach the banking system only through the platform's rails. When a dollar price moves away from par, users, price feeds and oracles need to know which of the two failed, and we know of no measure that separates them. This is hard because a ledger's value is never quoted directly, public prices are asynchronous last trades that thin out under stress, and any single asset may carry its own shock. We price the platform's dollar through unpegged assets against venues whose rails stay open, which splits a dollar-quoted dislocation into a token and a ledger component, and we accept the split only when unrelated assets agree and the venue's internal cross-rates hold. We apply it to rail-cut episodes on three platforms: three Bitfinex windows from 2017 to 2019, Binance.US in 2023, and Binance's sterling and euro rails. On Bitfinex the platform's dollar fell by up to 844, 610 and 627 bps (daily medians), with BTC and ETH agreeing to within 7.2 bps and internal cross-rates holding to within 8 bps. Binance.US shows the same signature in three assets. On both platforms the dollar traded at a discount while exit was impaired and at a premium in a later phase (up to 592 bps on Bitfinex in 2017), and the gaps closed when the episodes ended. In the March 2023 USDC run, by contrast, the method attributes all but 6% of the dislocation to the token, and an hourly monitor flags no SVB or FTX hour as a ledger failure. The sterling and euro cuts show only small effects. All findings are descriptive.

**Suggested keywords:** stablecoins; platform money; exchange ledgers; price feeds and oracles; Web measurement; natural experiment; reproducibility
